source.title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions

accepted.question_text: In relativistic heavy-ion collisions that aim to create and characterize a quark-gluon plasma, what is the best model for the fluctuating initial state, and what constraints can existing flow and particle-correlation data already place on that model?
accepted.context_brief: Initial-state model selection and data constraints

evidence.quote:
Specific questions that were addressed during this workshop include:
• What is the best model for the initial state? What constraints can we already put
on it from new data?

there is not a
binary choice between two well understood competing models for the initial condition
(e.g., ’Glauber’ versus ’CGC’), as is sometimes inferred by those not directly involved
in this research, but instead there exists a large space of possible physical pictures,
parameters, and implementations.

accepted.question_text: How is event-by-event initial spatial anisotropy in the transverse density of a heavy-ion collision converted by the system evolution into final-state momentum anisotropy of detected particles, and can this hydrodynamic response be understood generally enough to avoid running a separate event-by-event hydrodynamic simulation for every candidate initial condition?

evidence.quote:
• How exactly is the initial spatial anisotropy converted to final-state momentum
anisotropy? Can we understand the hydrodynamic response in general, or do we
need to run event-by-event hydrodynamic simulations for every candidate initial
condition?

The elliptic asymmetry in the initial state is transformed during the
collective expansion into an asymmetry in the final momentum distribution of the
detected particles.

accepted.question_text: What is the current uncertainty in the viscosity and transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma inferred from anisotropic-flow observables, and what strategy would best reduce that uncertainty?

evidence.quote:
• What is the current uncertainty in the viscosity of the QGP, and what is the best
strategy for reducing it?

Some questions arose as to how a meaningful comparison to theory calculations can
and should be performed, which is crucial for any quantitative statements about the
transport coefficients of the quark gluon plasma.

accepted.question_text: What can newly measured heavy-ion observables, including new flow and particle-correlation observables, teach researchers about the quark-gluon plasma, the initial state, and the system evolution, and what additional observables should be measured?
accepted.context_brief: Interpretation and selection of new observables

evidence.quote:
• What else can the newly-measured observables teach us, and what other observables
should be measured?

These new measurements have the potential to provide tight constraints on theory
and to extract precise quantitative properties of the QGP, as well as to shed light on
the (as-yet poorly understood) non-equilibrium QCD dynamics of the initial stage of
the collision.

accepted.question_text: How can experimental measurements and theoretical calculations distinguish correlations caused by initial-state effects from correlations generated by collective final-state evolution in relativistic heavy-ion collisions?

evidence.quote:
• What are the prospects for experimentally and/or theoretically distinguishing
between initial-state and collective effects?

The extensive
factorization tests of two-particle correlations (Vn∆) over a large range of trigger and
associated particle transverse momentum as carried out by the LHC collaborations are
useful to distinguish bulk anisotropies from other/non-flow contributions, as well as
to study flow fluctuations.

accepted.question_text: Can the various sources of event-by-event fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions, including fluctuations in nucleon or quark positions, binary interactions, finite nucleon extent, initial momentum distribution, and local energy deposition or particle production, be disentangled from one another?

evidence.quote: • Can one disentangle various sources of fluctuations?

The following sources of fluctuations were studied here:
• Fluctuations in the positions of the nucleons (or quarks) and their binary
interactions
• Finite extent of the nucleons and correspondingly adjusted Wood-Saxon
distributions
• Fluctuations in the initial momentum distribution (initial flow)
• Local fluctuations in energy deposition/particle production

accepted.question_text: How should the longitudinal direction in fluctuating initial-state profiles be modeled and constrained in 3+1-dimensional viscous hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collisions, given that existing studies of longitudinal fluctuations remain exploratory and η- and Δη-dependent particle correlations may provide useful information?

evidence.quote:
Since
there are more and more 3+1 dimensional (viscous) hydrodynamic codes in use, it is
definitely time to pay more attention to the longitudinal direction. There have been
a few exploratory studies on longitudinal fluctuations [10, 11], but a comprehensive
understanding is still missing. The η and ∆η dependence of particle correlations can
lead to useful insights in that respect.

accepted.question_text: Can rapid thermalization during the initially non-equilibrium stage of a heavy-ion collision be obtained in an SU(3) Yang-Mills field-evolution framework when quantum fluctuations are included in a full 3+1-dimensional simulation?
accepted.context_brief: Rapid thermalization in initial non-equilibrium evolution

evidence.quote:
The initial non-equilibrium evolution is still one of the main open questions in
the field. Recently, there was a new promising attempt using SU(3) Yang-Mills field
evolution by the BNL group [12]. It will be particularly interesting to see if rapid
thermalization can be obtained within this framework by including quantum fluctuations
in a full 3+1D simulation.

accepted.question_text: What are the size and importance of initial flow—the initial velocity or momentum fields produced before hydrodynamic evolution—and how should the complete energy-momentum tensor, including shear-stress components, be used to initialize hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collisions?

evidence.quote:
Since the initial evolution produces finite initial velocity fields, a complete energy￾momentum tensor including shear stress components should be used to initialize the
hydrodynamic evolution. There are a few studies on the influence of initial flow in the
system, but a consensus on its size and importance has not been reached yet.

accepted.question_text: Beyond the first few coordinate-space Fourier coefficients ε_n used to characterize initial-state profiles, what additional quantities can represent the longitudinal structure, initial velocity profile, and other initial-state features more completely?

evidence.quote:
At the moment, the primary means of characterizing initial state profiles is
calculation of the first few coefficients of the Fourier expansion in coordinate space
(ǫn). It needs to be explored whether there are other quantities that are suitable for

representing the longitudinal direction, the initial velocity profile and other features in
a more complete way.

accepted.question_text: How can data and modeling constrain the scale and amplitude of initial-state fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions, such as flux-tube radius, Gaussian width, or correlation length, while tying those constraints to a specified physical assumption about the initial state?

evidence.quote:
Overall, the main task at hand is to constrain the scale of the fluctuations
exemplified by flux-tube radius, gaussian width, and the amplitude of fluctuations or
correlation length [13] in connection with a specific physics assumption.

accepted.question_text: Can a single theoretical calculation describe multiple heavy-ion observables in detail, including several flow harmonics v_n{2} as functions of transverse momentum and centrality, higher cumulants, and both hard and soft physics over a large transverse-momentum range?

evidence.quote:
In the future it will be necessary to describe multiple observables from a single
calculation, as well as to do so in more detail. At a minimum, a simultaneous description
of multiple flow harmonics vn{2} is needed as a function of transverse momentum and
centrality, with even more information contained in higher cumulants [14]. Especially
challenging is a combined understanding of hard and soft physics, allowing for a
description over a large range in transverse momentum [7].

accepted.question_text: Which aspects of fluctuating initial conditions is each final-state observable most sensitive to, and can a general characterization of hydrodynamic medium response be developed well enough to place significant constraints on both initial conditions and quark-gluon-plasma medium properties?
accepted.context_brief: Observable sensitivity and general medium response

evidence.quote:
Motivated by the large uncertainties that still remain in the initial conditions,
another emerging theme is the characterization of the medium response in a general
way. A more detailed understanding of hydrodynamic response to initial conditions, as
well as a precise determination of which aspects of the initial conditions each observable
is most sensitive to, would allow for significant constraints to be placed on the properties
of the initial conditions [24] and medium properties [25].

accepted.question_text: How far can simplified response relations between initial eccentricities and final flow harmonics be pushed—for example, can all mixed-harmonic event-plane correlations be reproduced without brute-force event-by-event hydrodynamic calculations?
accepted.context_brief: Limits of simplified hydrodynamic response relations

evidence.quote:
An open question remains as to
how far this can be pushed — e.g., can one reproduce all of the mixed harmonic event
plane correlations without resorting to brute force event-by-event calculations?

This is providing us with important insight, but it is
an open question how far this can be taken and whether brute-force event-by-event
calculations will always be necessary for describing certain data.

accepted.question_text: How should theoretical calculations and experimental analyses define and match centrality classes so that comparisons between heavy-ion data and models yield meaningful quantitative statements about quark-gluon-plasma transport coefficients, especially when impact parameter, initial gluon number, entropy production, and final particle yields must be related?

evidence.quote:
Some questions arose as to how a meaningful comparison to theory calculations can
and should be performed, which is crucial for any quantitative statements about the
transport coefficients of the quark gluon plasma.

This mapping procedure needs to be carefully cross-checked, especially when
the evolution is dissipative and the entropy increases. Differing centrality selection
criteria can significantly influence the results, and any assumptions relating the impact
parameter to the number of gluons and the final particle yields needs to be verified.

accepted.question_text: How should theoretical calculations of final-state particle distributions be analyzed so that flow observables from hydrodynamic or hybrid simulations are compared apples-to-apples with experimental measurements, including scalar-product, two-particle correlation, cumulant, and event-plane methods?

evidence.quote:
For an apples-to-apples comparison it is important to
be aware of the different measurement methods and what they actually imply.

Keeping in mind caveats such as this, the best way to make a meaningful comparison
between theoretical calculations and experimental data is to employ the same analysis
as used by the experiments.

accepted.question_text: What future measurements of two-particle-correlation factorization, trigger and associated pseudorapidity dependence, and flow coefficients measured relative to event planes of different harmonic order should be used to distinguish bulk anisotropies from non-flow effects, study flow fluctuations, and probe hydrodynamic mode mixing?
accepted.context_brief: Future measurements for non-flow and mode mixing

evidence.quote:
The extensive
factorization tests of two-particle correlations (Vn∆) over a large range of trigger and
associated particle transverse momentum as carried out by the LHC collaborations are
useful to distinguish bulk anisotropies from other/non-flow contributions, as well as
to study flow fluctuations. Similar analyses can be done in the space of trigger and
associated pseudorapidity. Measurements of vn coefficients with respect to an event
plane of different order Ψm with m 6= n are sensitive to the hydrodynamic response and
give insights about mode-mixing.

accepted.question_text: Can the rapidity-even first-order event plane Ψ_1 be reconstructed experimentally, and what would such a reconstruction reveal about the corresponding rapidity-even v_1 flow observable in heavy-ion collisions?

evidence.quote:
Reconstructing the Ψ1 event plane that corresponds
to the rapidity-even v1 observable would be desirable.

accepted.question_text: Can untriggered two-particle correlations in events containing a 50–100 GeV jet, compared against minimum-bias events with a consistent centrality selection, provide insight into the interplay between jet-medium response and pure bulk-evolution effects?

evidence.quote:
Another measurement that could
provide insights into the interplay of jet-medium response and pure bulk evolution
effects is to analyse the untriggered two-particle correlations in events that contain
a 50-100 GeV jet and compare the result to the minimum bias one. One issue that
might complicate such a measurement is to find a consistent centrality selection, since
the requirement of a high momentum jet biases the event sample.

accepted.question_text: Can theory calculations of three-particle correlations with a high-transverse-momentum trigger particle and low-transverse-momentum associated particles, in Δφ–Δφ, Δφ–Δη, and Δη–Δη angular spaces, disentangle jet-medium effects from the underlying pure medium response?

evidence.quote:
The wish-list for the theory community is to calculate for example 3-particle
correlations with a high transverse momentum (6−8 GeV) trigger particle and associated

particles below ∼ 2 GeV in all different combinations of angular spaces, i.e. ∆φ − ∆φ,
∆φ−∆η and ∆η−∆η. As a baseline the correlation functions from a medium evolution
only would be interesting already. Otherwise, these multi-particle calculations are the
most promising way to disentangle jet-medium effects from the underlying pure medium
response, if such a distinction makes sense.

accepted.question_text: What is the physical meaning of the event-plane correlations measured by the ATLAS collaboration, and can additional theory comparisons clarify their interpretation?

evidence.quote:
The meaning of the event-plane correlations
as measured by the ATLAS collaboration should be investigated further by more theory
comparisons.

accepted.question_text: Can theoretical calculations of additional fluctuation and flow observables, including mean transverse-momentum fluctuations, higher-harmonic flow coefficients at lower beam energies and for different nuclei, and flow results for identified particles, be produced with sufficient statistics to constrain the number of initial-state sources and extend comparisons beyond top-energy collisions?

evidence.quote:
In addition, more theoretical effort needs to be spent on calculating other
fluctuation observables, such as hpT i fluctuations, that have sensitivity to the number
of sources in the initial state.

Another goal that might be easier
to reach is to perform calculations of higher harmonic flow coefficients at lower beam
energies, since there are now results available from the low beam energy scan at RHIC,
as well as for other nuclei (copper and uranium). The flow results for identified particles
should also be addressed by more theoretical calculations.

accepted.question_text: How should the field standardize initial-state model implementations, initial-anisotropy definitions ε_n, Glauber Monte Carlo variations, and experimental flow analyses so that heavy-ion results can be compared consistently across models and measurements?
accepted.context_brief: Standardization of models, definitions, and analyses

evidence.quote:
Once the ingredients
are better understood and there is a consensus reached on how to implement the
fluctuations and geometry, it would be beneficial for standardized versions of the models
to be made available to the public.

More standardization
is necessary in the field. Examples include definitions of initial anisotropies ǫn, variations
of Glauber Monte Carlo models, and experimental flow analyses.
